overview: The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire, united by Modu Chanyu in 209 BCE and ruling Mongolia and the lands to its west for three centuries. Their mounted archers, tribute treaties with Han China and left-and-right administration set the pattern for the Turkic and Mongol empires that followed.

items.text: Composite bows of horn and sinew, shot from the saddle, made every herdsman a warrior.
Bronze and iron for weapons and harness; gold plaques of animals in combat for the elite.
The chanyu ruled under Heaven, Tengri, with shamans and seasonal gatherings to sacrifice to ancestors, heaven and earth.
Elite tombs at Noin-Ula held Chinese silks, lacquer and Bactrian textiles beside the dead.
The heqin treaties from 198 BCE brought Han princesses, silk, grain and wine to the chanyu as the price of peace.
The Xiongnu taxed the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin and traded horses and furs to China.
The Xiongnu model of steppe empire was followed by the Turkic khaganates and the Mongols.
Their name may lie behind the Huns of European sources, though the link is unproven.

fall.text: The confederation split into southern and northern halves in 54 BCE. Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89 CE, and by 93 the Xianbei had taken over the steppe; the Southern Xiongnu lived on as Han clients inside the Great Wall.
